full_text:
Marta Schaaf, Amnesty International’s program director for climate, social justice and corporate accountability, said Wednesday in a statement that the extreme heat driving wildfires, drought and floods across multiple continents amounts to a human rights emergency. She urged national governments to protect people now and to confront the fossil fuel industry Amnesty blames for the crisis.
Schaaf tied the crisis to corporate greed and government failure. “This heat is political… It is a human rights emergency that threatens the rights to life, health, housing, water and sanitation, food, education, and a healthy environment.” She added that “[t]hese harms are being made worse by authoritarian tactics that attack climate science, restrict protest, spread climate disinformation and shield powerful fossil fuel interests from accountability.” She described extreme heat as “a multiplier of human rights harm,” rather than a stand-alone disaster.
Amnesty’s statement lands amid mounting evidence of the toll that extreme heat has taken globally. The World Health Organization’s heat-and-health fact sheet says the number of people exposed to extreme heat is climbing steeply in every region this century. It estimates roughly 489,000 heat-related deaths annually between 2000 and 2019. It also finds that heat mortality among people over 65 rose about 85 percent over two decades.
Those figures go in tandem with a summer of heat records in 2026. Successive heat domes have put tens of millions of Americans under heat alerts, and federal data show the contiguous United States recorded its second-hottest first half of any year in 2026. In Europe, French authorities attributed several thousand excess deaths to a June heatwave. Later, wildfires forced the evacuation of more than 325,000 people in France and Spain, among the worst blazes in France since the Second World War. Tunisia’s meteorological service recorded temperatures near 50 degrees Celsius, including a 49.7-degree reading in Kairouan that broke a regional record. Researchers at Istanbul Technical University reported that Türkiye is experiencing its most intense heatwaves in 75 years. In India, a recent study estimated that a single day of extreme heat corresponds with roughly 3,400 excess deaths nationwide. In Bangladesh, a 2025 World Bank report estimated that heat cost the economy 250 million lost workdays and US$1.78 billion in 2024. Moreover, a recent survey of Dhaka’s informal workers found nearly three-quarters said rising temperatures had eroded their health and incomes. Canadian fire agencies, meanwhile, recorded more active wildfires and a larger burned area than in either of the past two years.
Amnesty paired its criticism with a two-part demand. In the near term, it called on governments to protect people through adaptation and climate-resilient public services. These include early warning systems, safe housing, access to water, and heat protections. In the long term, it called for making polluters pay, defending climate science and civic space, and delivering a rapid, fully funded and equitable phase-out of fossil fuels. This call particularly affects US President Donald Trump’s administration. The Trump administration began a second US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement in January 2025, a move Amnesty warned set a disturbing precedent. In March 2025, Trump withdrew the US from the board of the UN climate loss-and-damage fund. The Trump administration did declare a national energy emergency on his first day in office. However, Trump also directed the Justice Department to challenge state climate laws, and moved to repeal the 2009 “endangerment finding” that underpins most federal climate regulation.

Extreme heat has emerged as one of the biggest threats to South Asia’s employment landscape with a latest World Bank report suggesting that soaring temperature wipes out about 31 million full-time jobs every year across the region while thwarting creation of more over the coming decades. In the report, ‘A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia’s Cities,’ the World Bank says South Asia must generate employment for nearly 280 million additional working-age people by 2050 and most of them in cities. For, rising temperatures are making outdoor work increasingly unsafe, depressing labour productivity, reducing earnings and discouraging investment needed to create new jobs.
The World Bank says that Indian cities are slated to lose job-equivalent working hours (JELs) over the next few decades as heat-related work hour loss will mount drastically. By 2030, New Delhi is projected to lose full-time equivalent jobs from 2.66 lakh in 2030 to 6.29 lakh by 2080. Kolkata could lose the equivalent of 8.33 lakh jobs by 2080 due to working hours lost to excessive heat, up from 3.6 lakh in 2030. Mumbai is projected to lose the equivalent of 2.7 lakh jobs by 2080, up from 2.04 lakh in 2030, while Chennai’s losses are expected to nearly double from 1.41 lakh to 2.69 lakh over the same period.
Similarly, Ahmedabad and Surat are estimated to lose 1.48 lakh and 1.37 lakh jobs respectively by 2080. Varanasi, though recording the lowest absolute losses, is projected to see its figures increase from 51,000 in 2030 to 1.25 lakh by 2080. Among other South Asian cities analysed, Dhaka is expected to be the worst affected, with job-equivalent losses rising from 4.65 lakh in 2030 to 16.5 lakh by 2080.
The estimates are based on a moderate-emissions scenario (SSP2-4.5) and translate lost working hours caused by unsafe heat exposure into the equivalent number of full-time jobs. The JEL is not actual employment losses but converts lost work hours due to heat exposure into the number of full-time jobs those hours would represent, providing a measure of the economic impact of rising temperatures.
India’s jobs engine under pressure
India is expected to account for a substantial share of South Asia’s expanding workforce over the next quarter century. However, the World Bank report warns that the country’s employment will face a heat challenge. It cites research showing that extreme heat is already reducing labour productivity across sectors ranging from agriculture and construction to street vending and manufacturing. It cited that 90% of New Delhi street vendors reduced working hours due to heat in summer 2025.
It cited one study which revealed rice harvesting productivity fell by around 5% for every degree Celsius increase above the safe Wet Bulb Globe Temperature threshold, while outdoor workers experienced substantially higher productivity losses under prolonged heat exposure. India has already warmed by 1.15 degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Between May 2024 and May 2025, the country recorded 62 days when temperatures exceeded the historical 90th percentile, while several regions witnessed temperatures above 45 degree C and heatwaves lasting over two weeks. Urbanisation is compounding the problem. Expanding concrete landscapes and shrinking green spaces are creating intense urban heat islands, with dense neighbourhoods remaining more than 10 degree C hotter than surrounding rural areas even at night. The Heat Watch Surat initiative found temperature variations of 4.8 degree C to 7.5 degree C within different parts of the city depending on vegetation and built-up density, highlighting the role of urban planning in mitigating heat exposure.
Infrastructure feeling the heat
India’s infrastructure is already beginning to buckle under rising temperatures, the report revealed. Electricity demand has surged as households increasingly rely on cooling. Air-conditioner sales rose by an estimated 34% between 2023 and 2024, while electricity demand touched a record 156 billion units in May 2024, logging a 15% jump over the corresponding month in the previous year. Yet the same temperatures driving demand are also weakening the power system. When temperatures cross 40 degree C, outages become 20%-50% more frequent and last 15%-60% longer, according to the report. Transport infrastructure is facing similar stress. The World Bank pointed to heat damage on the Mumbai-Nagpur Expressway caused by unsuitable asphalt specifications. It also warned that Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport could experience temperatures approaching 50 degree C for multiple days every year by 2030, affecting aircraft lift, engine performance and passenger as well as cargo carrying capacity. Public transport services in cities such as Kolkata have already been disrupted as heat-related illnesses among drivers and declining passenger demand force operational changes.
Healthcare infrastructure remains poorly prepared. A survey of 623 healthcare facilities in India found 44% had no heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, while only 7% had central air-conditioning, exposing vulnerable patients to dangerous indoor temperatures during heatwaves.
Crisis spanning South Asia
The report says the challenge extends well beyond India. South Asia has already warmed by an average of 1.26 degree C above pre-industrial levels, with Bhutan, Bangladesh and Nepal recording even higher increases. Climate models indicate the Himalayan region will experience the fastest warming this century, while coastal cities will become increasingly hot and humid.
By 2070, around 520 million people across the region are expected to face at least one month of dangerous heat each year which is four times the number exposed today. The report argues that the real human toll is likely much higher than official statistics suggest because heat-related deaths are often recorded as cardiac or renal failure. Working-hour losses are projected to rise sharply across South Asia by 2080. Annual productivity losses could reach 7.4% in Dhaka, 6.3% in Patna, 4.4% in Chattogram, 3.7% in Colombo, 2.9% in Jaipur and 0.7% in Kathmandu. The economic consequences are also equally stark. Without adaptation, the World Bank estimates South Asia’s GDP could be nearly 7% smaller by 2050, representing the largest projected loss among developing regions. Informal workers are expected to bear the greatest burden, with incomes falling by around 40% during severe heatwaves as working hours decline and expenditure on water, cooling and healthcare rises.

It will be the first time among Japan's six passenger railway companies that customer-facing employees will be allowed to wear polo shirts as part of their work attire.
Made of 100% polyester, the shirts retain the design of the company's previous short-sleeved shirts while improving breathability and sweat absorption. Employees will wear them tucked into their trousers.
Other railway operators are also moving toward more casual uniforms. Eizan Railway in Kyoto introduced polo shirts on a trial basis this month for train operators and station staff.
A company official said, "We hope to improve work efficiency by creating a more comfortable working environment."
Odakyu Railway introduced polo shirts made by Uniqlo as uniforms in August last year. This year, the company expanded the policy to part-time employees, allowing them to wear the shirts from June 1 through the end of October.
Hotels Rethink Summer Workwear
The RIHGA Royal Hotel Osaka Vignette Collection introduced summer uniforms for doormen as part of a broader redesign of staff attire.
Worn from June through October, the uniforms combine short sleeves with a vest, while the trousers are made with materials that offer UV protection, quick-drying properties and a cooling effect.
A hotel spokesperson said, "The uniforms are designed to help staff work comfortably while maintaining the formal appearance expected of hotel employees."
Cleanliness Over Formality
A June survey by Onward Holdings of men and women in their 20s to 60s nationwide asked what makes work clothes look "appropriate" on extremely hot days. The most common response was "a sense of cleanliness," cited by 62.3% of respondents, while "formality" ranked lowest at 16.7%.
Even companies without specific heat-related dress rules are taking a more flexible approach. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. has introduced a "dress code free" policy that allows employees to choose their clothing based on the time, place, and occasion.
Financial services group Resona Group also allows employees to work without ties or jackets, or to wear polo shirts, while taking workplace situations and customer interactions into consideration.

Summer in Thailand can feel endless, with the hot weather varying between dry and wet seasons. Thai locals are experts at living with high temperatures – and useful guides on how to beat the heat, keep cool and look good all year round. We asked three busy Bangkok tastemakers, working across art, music, retail and culture, to open their suitcases and share their summer travel plans.
Pranitan ‘Pete’ Phornprapha
CEO and founder, Scratch First
Scratch First is the company behind the Wonderfruit music festival. Thailand’s answer to Glastonbury or Burning Man is a December fixture on the region’s calendar. This year, Phornphrapha is spreading his wings to Japan with Chapters Kyoto, a cultural gathering debuting in October. The four-day event for 100 ticketholders promises to be as unique and unmissable as the inaugural Wonderfruit in 2014.
Favourite ice cream?
Watermelon and salted fish crumbs. It’s a Thai delicacy and usually [eaten as] an appetiser. I tried it at an ice-cream shop in Pattani, [a city in southern Thailand].
Beach or mountains?
Always mountains. I like skiing and hiking. I like the energy. I feel more grounded in the mountains.
Where are you heading this summer?
I just came back from Switzerland – [first to] Villars-sur-Ollon, then Gstaad. It was a short trip to send the kids to summer camp but I always like to leave time to explore. Then it’s Shanghai to send off my other daughter, followed by the Maldives for a real holiday.
Why the Maldives?
I like snorkelling, scuba diving and surfing. It’s shoulder season, so the waves should be good. In the Maldives you can surf in the middle of the ocean, right between the islands.
Where will you stay?
Soneva Fushi. It’s the original Soneva and barefoot-luxury pioneer. It’s important to choose the right island and I like going to the natural ones that are slightly more remote, wild and lush. Very Robinson Crusoe.
What’s in your suitcase?
Shorts, swimming trunks and sunglasses – classic Ray Bans and a Japanese brand called Nackymade. I’m a creature of habit, so I wear the same labels. Industry of All Nations does basics really well. Its products are all naturally dyed.
What are you reading or watching?
I read four or five books at a time and skip around. I was given The Hidden Life of Trees and my partner bought me Empire of Pain about the Sackler family. I picked up Strange Parallels: Southeast Asia in Global Context, c. 800-1830; it’s very academic but I want a deeper understanding of this region.
Any essentials?
My diary. I write a lot, I always have. I found my current journal at Pettinaroli in Milan. It’s leather bound and I really like it. I don’t bring my computer when I’m on holiday. I check in with work a little bit but I usually do calls.
Who’s on your holiday playlist?
There’s this English electronic jazz band called Portico Quartet and one of the members [Jack Wyllie] has a special project called Paradise Cinema. He collaborated with a Senegalese musician. Gorgeous cinematic jazz featuring West African instruments.
Anything to drink?
I like my wine chilled and crisp. Someone recently introduced me to a beautiful white rioja. Burgundy for reds and mezcal for a little more fun.
Adulaya ‘Kim’ Hoontrakul
Director, Bangkok Art and Culture Centre
Art historian Kim Hoontrakul became the youngest director of the Bangkok Art and Culture Centre in 2022. Her stewardship has given the publicly funded contemporary-arts centre fresh relevance. Hoontrakul is one of the four curators of the next Bangkok Art Biennale, which opens on 29 October 2026. Exhibitions under the theme “Angels and Mara” will be on show across various venues in the Thai capital until 28 February 2027.
Favourite ice cream?
Mint chocolate.
What’s your local getaway?
Scuba diving. Any chance I get, I will do a quick escape to one of the islands. Koh Tao is one of the best diving spots and it’s never the same dive. I fly from Bangkok to Koh Samui, then take a boat.
Beach or mountains?
Definitely both. My instinct is always the beach, but for the past 10 years I’ve been doing a lot of trekking. Walking along a path gives a whole different type of view. One of my most memorable treks was in Sikkim, India.
Where are you heading this summer?
The Sā Ladakh Biennale is this August. It only lasts 10 days and you trek through all of these villages [in Ladakh]. I’m still optimistic that I can find time to go. Either way, I’ll be in Italy in September for a roadtrip through the Dolomites.
What’s in your suitcase?
If I’m diving, my dive gear. If I’m trekking, my Fastpack shoes from The North Face. If it’s just a city break, [then I pack] an array of outfits because I am an overpacker and I must have all options for every kind of weather. My holiday clothes are an amalgamation of everything that I’ve picked up on my travels. I challenged myself to do a 10-day trip to Okinawa with only hand luggage and it was the worst experience of my life. Never again. I will gladly lug around a giant suitcase.
How about your beach bag?
I just transfer [the contents of] my normal day bag – [my] Kindle, AirPods, sunblock and sunglasses – into my huge beach tote, a lime-green Loewe shopper. I stopped buying designer sunglasses and now I only go for specialist eyewear brands. My Ray Bans have served me well for the past five years.
What’s on your Kindle?
So many half-read books. I’ve been trying to finish Possession, which is about all the looted artworks that are scattered across the Western world, but I keep getting distracted by memoirs. I’m really into provocative writers with a strong, obnoxious voice. I’ve just finished Problems by Jade Sharma. It’s about one part of the author’s life when she was a drug addict. I connected [to the story] as a woman, it helped me to understand addiction and it was a nice break from reading academic papers.
Any essentials?
My red Gucci horsebit loafers and a handheld fan. It’s so strong it can almost blow dry my hair. I bought it for a trip to the Netherlands earlier this year, at the start of the heatwave. Europe has no concept of air conditioning so I had to be prepared.
What’s to drink?
Iced tea.
Paul Sirisant
CEO, Cloud 11
DJ and former executive of Universal Music Thailand, Paul Sirisant jumped into the world of real estate when he was appointed CEO of Cloud 11. The Snøhetta-designed mixed-used development in Bangkok opened in July with offices tailored to production studios and spaces for musicians, filmmakers, designers and other creatives, along with a shopping mall and hotels. Interested to learn more? Sirisant will be speaking at The Monocle Quality of Life Conference in Lisbon this year. Book your ticket here.
Favourite ice cream?
Rum and raisin. A good amount of rum without getting drunk.
How do you escape the heat in Bangkok?
I go wing foiling. When the ground gets too hot, it produces thermal heat and that becomes thermal wind. There’s a great lake in Bangkok about 10km away from Sukhumvit, while Hua Hin has some of the best thermal wind anywhere in the world.
Where are you heading this summer?
I usually take my family to England. We have a place in Taplow near Windsor. The kids love driving around with the windows down and breathing the fresh air. And Legoland is 15 minutes from where we live. No frills, no long lines, hassle free.
What’s in your suitcase?
Timo boardshorts and two pairs of sunglasses – Oakleys for running and Oliver Peoples for chilling. I have a habit of buying vintage T-shirts from the Red Building in Chatuchak and cutting off the sleeves to create some air flow. That’s my summer thing and it drives my kids crazy.
What will you be reading?
The memoire Liberation Through Hearing by Richard Russell, the founder of XL Recordings. I like contemporary music history. This same guy was behind The Prodigy, The XX, Dizzee Rascal and Adele. How crazy is that?
Any essentials?
Rekordbox. It’s an integrated DJ software that I have on my phone. The app is connected to my sets and I have it with me all the time. I’m still DJing after 30 years and I’m very particular about how I organise my music. I colour-code each song by energy level.
What’s on your summer playlist?
I have a bad habit of trying to DJ for my family in the car. I queue songs that I want to introduce my kids to based on what they are listening to. They have gotten into Japanese rock through watching anime, so I’m going to play something with the same range, such as Muse. I fall in love with new music all the time. I listened to Kelsey Lu recently after reading an interview with them in a magazine.
What are you drinking?
Natural orange wine during the day because it cleans the palate. At night, if I’m out, I love white spirits. Gin, tequila or vodka with soda. Clean and light, day or night.
Top tip for keeping cool?
Understand the wind. Learn how it flows in each season and how it changes. I am a surfer and, no matter where I am, I figure out the wind direction.

Four people died after extremely heavy rain triggered landslides in Kerala's southern districts, with rescue teams deployed as the weather system shifts north.
Four people have died after extremely heavy rainfall measuring up to 361 mm in 24 hours triggered a series of landslides and debris flows in Keralam's southern districts, officials said on Saturday. According to Sekhar Lukose Kuriakose, Member Secretary of the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA), two fatalities each have been reported from Idukki and Kottayam districts. The intense rain spell, which occurred primarily between 10 PM and early morning, caused significant damage to houses and roads in slope-cut areas.
"So essentially, what we have seen is fatality numbers are very low, thankfully. We have two deaths reported from Idukki and two from Kottayam," he said.
"Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Idukki experienced extremely heavy rainfall measuring up to 361 mm at places in the last maybe 24 hours or so. Much of the rain spell was after about 10 o'clock at night and until the early morning. That has caused a number of landslides in slope-cut faces where there are roads and houses and all that. And we have also seen some debris flows happening here and there. It's just a cloudburst, that's it. Nothing else, nothing big," Kuriakose added.
The official described the weather phenomenon simply as a "cloudburst". He noted that while the rainfall was unprecedented — stating that no river could contain 361 mm of rain in less than 12 hours — the fatality numbers remained low due to high public awareness and prior alerts. Providing a weather update, Kuriakose added, "The rain spell for the south is almost over. Now it's moving towards the north. It has started raining, so starting from Thrissur to Kasaragod today also we will experience significant amounts of rainfall until tomorrow. And after that, we will have a respite from this extremely heavy rainfall situation."
On the rescue front, nine NDRF teams have been pre-positioned in districts including Pathanamthitta, Idukki, and Alappuzha. Kuriakose emphasised the role of local agencies and volunteers, noting that approximately 10,000 'Aapda Mitra' volunteers and an equal number of Civil Defence personnel are working alongside the Fire and Rescue services.
"They all work in tandem with the fire and rescue service, and they coordinate. So while the might of fire and rescue is seen to be undermined many a time, they are our workhorses, you know. They are the ones who are really extending their arms to every part of Kerala. NDRFs are essentially meant for the last mile, you know, that extra edge when you have difficulties in cutting across certain places," he said.
In view of the continuing rainfall, Keralam Health Minister K Muraleedharan directed the Health Department to convene an emergency meeting of officials today. The meeting, scheduled for 11 am, will be held online and chaired by Health Department Director Meenakshi. The emergency session, which will include District Medical Officers and NHM District Programme Managers, aims to review the functioning of relief camps and discuss local-level medical arrangements. Further action will be determined after assessing the specific needs of each affected district.

In Idukki district, a landslide at Adurmala in Kudayathoor near Thodupuzha buried a house, killing Sumathi, a resident of Mashikkallel House.

Several other landslides were reported across Idukki and Kottayam. At Mathayippara in Upputhara, a landslide struck a police jeep, although officers escaped after stepping out of the vehicle moments earlier.
Minor landslides were also reported at Nellappara in Karinkunnam, and near Mankombu Temple in Moonnilavu and Payyanithottam in Poonjar.
Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan said the state government is coordinating rescue and relief efforts as heavy rain continues to affect several districts.
The Chief Minister said he held discussions with the Revenue Minister, Chief Secretary and district collectors following reports of landslides and mudslides.
The Revenue Minister will coordinate disaster management activities, while a meeting of district collectors has been convened to review the situation.
The government has placed the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), police and other emergency teams on standby to handle any developing situation. Authorities have also been directed to ensure better treatment for the injured and speed up rehabilitation efforts.
Sekhar Lukose Kuriakose, Member Secretary of the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) said Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Idukki received exceptionally heavy rainfall, with some areas recording up to 361mm in 24 hours.
Most of the rain fell between 10pm and the early hours of Saturday, triggering landslides, damaging houses and roads, and causing debris flows.
"It was essentially a cloudburst. Nothing else, nothing bigger," he said, adding that no river could safely contain such an intense volume of rainfall within a few hours.
Despite the severity of the weather, Kuriakose said timely alerts and increased public awareness helped keep casualties relatively low.
Pathanamthitta recorded more than 300mm of rainfall within just two hours, according to District Collector Nizamudeen A.
The intense downpour caused the Pamba River to overflow, submerging parts of Ranni town under waist-deep floodwater.
Police, Fire and Rescue Services, revenue officials and local panchayat teams are carrying out evacuation and rescue operations.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued weather alerts as heavy rain continues across the state.
An orange alert remains in place for Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Palakkad, Malappuram, Thrissur, Ernakulam and Idukki, with 12cm to 20cm of rainfall forecast within 24 hours.
